Cyril of Jerusalem
SEER-il
proper noun
Greek Kyrillos, “lordly” or “of the Lord,” bishop of Jerusalem in the fourth century, author of the Catechetical Lectures.

📖 Biblical Definition

Cyril was bishop of Jerusalem in the fourth century, and his Catechetical Lectures, delivered to those preparing for baptism, are among the most precious witnesses we have to how the early church instructed its converts. He led the candidates step by step through the articles of the faith, the creed, the Scriptures, and the moral law, that they might come to baptism understanding what they professed. The dictionary honours this careful catechizing of converts, holding, as Cyril did, that the faith is to be taught and understood, not merely felt. Yet his lectures, especially the mystagogical addresses on the sacraments, show the sacramental theology of the church already drifting toward errors the Reformation had to correct: a heightened language about the bread and the cup, and a tendency to bind grace too tightly to the rite of baptism. Against such drift the dictionary holds the Lord’s own word, that it is the Spirit that quickeneth, the flesh profiteth nothing (Joh 6:63), and the Supper a remembrance that shews the Lord’s death till he come (1Co 11:24; 1Co 11:26). Cyril the catechist is honoured for his diligent teaching of the faith; the seeds of sacramental error in his lectures are weighed and refused by the rule of the word.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A fourth-century bishop of Jerusalem whose Catechetical Lectures model the instruction of converts, though tending to sacramental error.

CYRIL OF JERUSALEM, bishop of Jerusalem in the fourth century.

His Catechetical Lectures instructed candidates preparing for baptism.

He led converts through the creed, the Scriptures, and the moral law.

His mystagogical lectures show a drift toward heightened sacramental language.

He is honoured as a catechist while his sacramental errors are weighed.

1Co 11:24 — "And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me."

1Co 11:26 — "For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord’s death till he come."

Joh 6:63 — "It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

His diligent catechizing is honoured, while the sacramental drift in his lectures is weighed and refused by the word.

expand to see more

What is honourable in Cyril is his catechizing, the patient instruction of converts in the creed, the Scriptures, and the moral law before they came to baptism. The dictionary honours this diligence, holding that the faith is to be taught and understood, and commending the church that does not receive members untaught.

The corruption to weigh is the sacramental drift his lectures display. Already in Cyril’s mystagogy the language about the bread and cup is heightened beyond the Scriptural memorial, and grace is bound too closely to the outward rite, sowing seeds that grew in later ages into the errors of transubstantiation and baptismal regeneration. Against this the dictionary holds that the Spirit quickeneth and the flesh profiteth nothing, that the Supper shews the Lord’s death as a remembrance, and that men are saved not by the bare washing but by the mercy of God and the renewing of the Holy Ghost. Cyril the catechist is received; the seeds of sacramental error in his lectures are refused.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Greek for “lordly,” Cyril of Jerusalem names the fourth-century bishop and catechist.

expand to see more

Cyril — Greek Kyrillos, “lordly” or “of the Lord.”

He was bishop of Jerusalem in the fourth century.

His Catechetical Lectures instructed candidates for baptism.

They witness to how the early church taught its converts.

They also show an early drift toward sacramental error.

Usage

"Like Cyril’s lectures, the church teaches its converts the faith before it receives them."

"It is the Spirit that quickeneth; the flesh, and the bare rite, profiteth nothing."

"The Supper is a remembrance that shews the Lord’s death till He come."
